rules.statement: Have the server generate every secret's material; a create request for a secret carries only metadata (type, key size, curve, use, algorithm, lifetimes) and never caller-supplied material.
rules.why: Generating on the server keeps material off the wire into the API. A caller-supplied value would make material something the caller controls.
rules.check: Look for create or update request contracts for secrets or keys with a field holding key bytes, a shared-secret value or a private key, and for handlers that store such a value instead of calling the secret generator.

rules.statement: Never return secret material from a read, list, import, update or preview path; only the create (or rotate) response of a secret whose owner has an external holder may reveal it, and only that one time.
rules.why: A path that returns material on read, or a cache holding that response, is a standing liability. Every later read, cache, log and audit record becomes a place the secret can leak from.
rules.check: Look for get, list, PUT, PATCH, import or preview handlers that return a response type carrying secret material, and for a new 'read secret' endpoint.

rules.statement: Model a one-time secret reveal as a distinct response type (the material-free resource plus the material), not as an optional, usually null material field on the resource type that reads return.
rules.why: An optional field on the type every read returns makes leakage a reviewing discipline problem. A separate type makes where a secret can appear structurally visible.
rules.check: Look for a nullable secret, material or plaintext property added to a shared resource or read DTO, or for a single response type reused by revealing and non-revealing endpoints.

rules.statement: Never return a key the server holds for itself (such as a tenant's signing or encryption key) or the private half of an asymmetric key pair over the API; the reveal decision is made first by owner, through the endpoint's response type, and only then by secret type.
rules.why: No party outside the server needs its own private keys. A server-minted private key handed back would exist only to be put on the wire; a client using private_key_jwt generates its own pair and registers the public half.
rules.check: Look for server-owned secret create endpoints returning the revealing type, for material set for generated asymmetric secrets, and for a reveal decided only by a runtime check on secret type.

rules.statement: Never write secret plaintext to an audit event, a log, a trace or the stored row.
rules.why: Each of these places outlives the one-time reveal and becomes a leak surface. A lost secret is recovered only by issuing another.
rules.check: Look for logging, audit, activity or telemetry calls, and for persistence mappings, that include a generated secret's plaintext or a revealing response object.

rules.statement: Treat secret material as immutable: an update endpoint changes metadata only, and a secret is replaced by creating a new one (or rotating it) and deleting the old one, never by a full-replace PUT that accepts material.
rules.why: A full-replace update would let a caller supply material and make material mutable.
rules.check: Look for update request types or handlers that accept or overwrite key material, or a PUT that replaces the whole secret.

rules.statement: Mark every endpoint whose response can carry a secret or a one-time credential (a revealed secret, a token, client_secret, registration_access_token, request_uri, device_code, user_code, auth_req_id) uncacheable with an endpoint filter applied at mapping time, which emits `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, max-age=0` and `Pragma: no-cache` before the handler runs.
rules.why: Headers written in each handler can be forgotten by a new route or an early return, and the mapping would no longer show which routes reveal a secret. A filter covers both success and error responses, and the extra directives cover HTTP/1.0 caches and caches that ignore no-store (RFC 6749 §5.1, RFC 7591 §3.2.1, RFC 9126, RFC 8628, CIBA).
rules.check: Look for a new or changed endpoint returning any of these values that isn't mapped with the no-store filter (for example `.WithNoStore()`), or one that sets cache headers by hand in the handler instead.

rules.statement: Apply the no-store filter to each secret-revealing endpoint individually rather than to a whole route group, and use an endpoint filter rather than a middleware that reads endpoint metadata.
rules.why: A group-wide filter misses endpoints outside the group and marks routes that other packages map into it. A middleware depends on how the host orders its middleware, and a filter does not.
rules.check: Look for no-store applied to a MapGroup or route group as a whole, or for new middleware that inspects endpoint metadata to set cache headers.

rules.statement: Don't report a missing no-store header on a response written before the endpoint filter runs, such as a 400 for a body that fails to bind or a 401 or 403 from an outer filter.
rules.why: Those responses carry no secret, so leaving them unmarked is intended.
rules.check: Before reporting, confirm the response is produced ahead of the endpoint filter and carries no secret or one-time credential.

rules.statement: A store method that adds, updates or removes one of an owner's secrets bumps the owner's secrets concurrency token, so that every replica reloads and the ETag/If-Match model sees the change.
rules.why: Without the bump, other replicas keep stale secrets and concurrency checks miss the change.
rules.check: Look for new or changed per-secret store mutations that don't update the owner's secrets concurrency token.

rules.statement: Keep secret generation and cryptography inside the dedicated secret generator abstraction, never in the management API package or a serializer.
rules.why: Spreading cryptography into a package that has none multiplies the code to audit.
rules.check: Look for key or random-secret generation (RandomNumberGenerator, RSA.Create, ECDsa.Create, and similar) in management or serialization code instead of a call to the secret generator.

rules.statement: In a test project, cover each secret-revealing route with an integration test that asserts the no-store cache headers, and cover the read paths with a test that asserts their responses carry no material.
rules.why: The tests are what guarantee that every revealing route stays uncacheable and that no read path leaks material.
rules.check: When a diff adds or changes a secret-revealing endpoint, look for a matching integration test that asserts Cache-Control and Pragma, and for a test of the material-free read response.
